name: Healthcare Use Case
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Drug Pedigrees and Patient Records: Where Blockchain Meets Regulation and Privacy Law
lesson.summary: Healthcare actually contains two very different blockchain stories: pharmaceutical supply chain verification, which has a real legal forcing function behind it, and patient medical records, where privacy law and provider incentives have mostly kept blockchain a research topic rather than a working system.
lesson.body:
It is easy to lump "blockchain in healthcare" together as one story, but it is really two, and they have gone very differently. The first is verifying that a specific package of medication is genuine and has moved legally through the supply chain from manufacturer to pharmacy. The second is making a patient's medical records portable and interoperable across different hospitals and providers. Both were pitched with similar enthusiasm around the same period, but one has a real regulatory forcing function behind it and the other largely does not, which turns out to matter enormously.

On the drug supply chain side, the United States' Drug Supply Chain Security Act requires an interoperable, electronic system for verifying prescription medications as they move between manufacturers, wholesalers, and pharmacies, specifically to catch counterfeit or diverted drugs. The MediLedger Network, built by a company called Chronicled with backing from major pharmaceutical manufacturers and distributors including Pfizer, Genentech, McKesson, and AmerisourceBergen, is a real, distributed-ledger-based system built to help member companies meet exactly this kind of verification requirement (readers should treat its current operational scale as something to verify independently, since that kind of detail changes over time). This case looks like the supply chain story from the previous chapter in miniature: the participants are many independent legal entities that do not want to cede control of a shared verification record to any single competitor among them, and there is a hard legal deadline forcing genuine participation rather than a voluntary consortium hoping everyone eventually joins.

Patient medical records tell a much less settled story. The pitch was appealing: a patient-controlled, portable health record that follows them between providers, replacing the fax machines and incompatible electronic health record systems that still slow down care coordination today. In practice, this use case has mostly stayed at the pilot or academic stage. Part of the reason is legal: privacy laws like HIPAA in the United States make putting actual patient health data on any kind of shared, widely-replicated ledger legally risky, so most serious proposals only put hashes or pointers on-chain and keep the real medical data in a conventional off-chain database anyway. Once that design choice is made, it becomes fair to ask what the blockchain layer is actually contributing that a well-permissioned centralized index could not. Existing electronic health record vendors also have limited financial incentive to make it easier for patients to move their data elsewhere. Estonia's health information system is frequently cited in blockchain marketing as a flagship example, using technology from a company called Guardtime known as KSI. It is worth being precise here: this system is best understood as a hash-based data integrity and timestamping mechanism controlled by a single vendor, rather than a multi-party consensus blockchain in the Bitcoin or Ethereum sense, and it is a good illustration of how loosely the word "blockchain" gets applied in healthcare marketing more broadly.

Running both stories through the case-study-analysis checklist from the previous chapter gives a clean answer. Drug pedigree verification involves genuine multi-party mistrust among independent companies plus a real regulatory deadline, which plausibly does need blockchain's specific properties. Patient medical records mostly do not clear that bar, because the real bottleneck has turned out to be legal and institutional rather than a missing shared-ledger technology, which is exactly the kind of distinction the blockchain definition itself should push you to make before accepting either use case at face value.
